# Results — Study 75 (Knee-Jerk) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — Connors
RSI(2) < 10 mean-reversion entry, exit when RSI(2) > 60 or after 10 days, no trend
filter — run on SPY and a basket of four large-cap equities (SPY, QQQ, AAPL, MSFT, JPM)
with daily bars since 1993–1999. Pinned against a **random-direction control** on the
*same* entry bars. Pre/post-publication split at 2009-01-01 (Connors & Alvarez book
published 2008, widely known by 2009). As-of **2026-06-12**; match the per-tape
fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## The honest test — gross (cost = 0), no trend filter

A direction-symmetric control (random entries on the *same* bars) decides whether
the RSI(2) signal knows something beyond "oversold usually bounces."

### SPY standalone

| Period | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **All (1993–2026)** | 803 | **76.2%** | **+62.1** | **+5.15** |
| Pre-2009 | 392 | 76.8% | +75.8 | +4.73 |
| Post-2009 | 411 | 75.7% | +49.0 | **+2.75** |
| Random control (all) | 803 | 66.5% | +29.2 | +3.37 |

- The RSI(2) gross expectancy on SPY is **+62.1 bps/trade** at HAC *t* = **+5.15** —
  well above the inference bar (|t| ≥ 2), firmly in **REAL** territory.
- It **beats the random control**: rule − random = **+32.9 bps/trade** (62.1 − 29.2).
  Even the random-direction arm earns a positive return (mean-reversion in SPY lifts all
  comers), but the RSI(2) signal adds a clear *extra* tilt.
- **Publication decay**: post-2009 mean drops from **+75.8 to +49.0 bps** (−35%), but
  remains statistically real (*t* = +2.75). The decay is real; the signal is not dead.

### Pooled basket (SPY + QQQ + AAPL + MSFT + JPM)

| Period | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **All** | 4,347 | **72.9%** | **+90.9** | **+10.70** |
| Pre-2009 | 2,111 | 74.5% | +106.6 | +7.87 |
| Post-2009 | 2,236 | 71.4% | +76.0 | **+7.36** |
| Random control | 4,347 | 63.3% | +33.5 | +5.83 |

- Pooled HAC *t* = **+10.70** (all) and **+7.36** (post-2009): the signal is unambiguously
  real and post-publication robust across the basket.
- Excess over random: **+57.4 bps/trade**, confirming the RSI(2) threshold adds
  directional information beyond the base-rate mean-reversion in equities.

## Could you trade it? — the cost sweep (SPY, post-2009)

With ~24 trades/yr, a per-trade round-trip cost barely dents the gross edge:

| round-trip cost | net mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* | ann. estimate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | +45.4 | +2.48 | +10.8%/yr |
| 2.0 bps | +43.4 | +2.37 | +10.3%/yr |
| 5.0 bps | +40.4 | +2.21 | +9.6%/yr |
| 10.0 bps | +35.4 | +1.94 | +8.4%/yr |

*Annualised estimate = mean\_bps × trades/yr ÷ 100; not a continuous-compounding backtest.*

The strategy is in the market ~34% of the time (~24 trades × 3.6-day average hold /
252). SPY buy-and-hold annualised +16.6%/yr over the same window — but the RSI(2) rule
earns +10.8% while being long only 34% of the time, an impressive capital efficiency.
At 10 bps the *t*-stat just falls below 2.0, marking the rough break-even of statistical
significance.

## The 200-SMA trend filter

Adding the trend filter (require price > SMA(200) to enter) cuts signal count from
411 to ~261/yr post-2009 and *reduces* the mean to +28.8 bps (t=+1.68 net at 2 bps).
The filter hurts: the best RSI(2) entries happen in drawdowns, which are often *below*
the 200-SMA. The canonical recipe's trend filter reduces the edge here.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works when there's something to find

On a deterministic synthetic daily tape, the same engine recovers an RSI(2) edge
**only when short-term anti-persistence is planted**, confirming the rule is a faithful
mean-reversion harvester, and that the real tape carries genuine short-term mean reversion:

| Planted reversion | rule gross (bps/trade) | beats random control? |
|---|--:|:--:|
| 0.00 (martingale) | ≈ noise | no |
| +0.15 (mild reversion) | positive | yes |
| +0.25 (strong reversion) | positive, larger | yes |
| −0.10 (momentum) | negative | no (wrong side) |

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL.** Gross HAC *t* = +5.15 on SPY (+2.75 post-2009), +10.70 pooled
  (+7.36 post-2009); beats random-direction control by +57.4 bps/trade. Every instrument
  above |*t*| = 2 (JPM weakest at +2.46). The mean-reversion effect is real and survives
  publication.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Signal decays post-2009 (−35% on SPY), and the strategy
  holds only a small fraction of the market's upside per unit of time invested. At
  realistic costs (~2–5 bps RT) the edge survives statistically but the ~10%/yr gross is
  not easily accessible: requires signal-level execution discipline and runs long-only in
  a market that has been going up. The trend filter — Connors' own addition — *reduces*
  performance here. Decayed, size-limited, and structurally long-only.
- **Decayed since publication? — CONFIRMED.** Pre-2009 mean +75.8 bps → post-2009
  +49.0 bps on SPY (−35%); the post-2009 signal is still real (*t* = +2.75) but clearly
  thinner.
